title: Psychosocial disability in Australia: Prevalence, functional severity and population projections to 2060 from repeated cross-sectional population surveys.
journal: The Australian and New Zealand journal of psychiatry
abstract: Existing approaches to estimating psychosocial disability - arising from severe mental illness - rely heavily on diagnostic categories and health service utilisation. By neglecting functional-limitation and participation restriction, such approaches limit the utility of current estimates for planning disability supports. This study addresses that gap by estimating the prevalence, functional severity and projected population counts of psychosocial disability in Australia, aligned with the World Health Organization International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health framework. Using a repeated cross-sectional design, we analysed four waves of the nationally representative Survey of Disability, Ageing and Carers (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018). Psychosocial disability was operationally defined as a long-term mental health condition combined with disability, consistent with the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health framework. Survey-weighted prevalence was estimated overall and by functional severity. Pooled age- and sex-specific prevalence rates were then applied to three population growth scenarios to project counts to 2060. Prevalence remained stable at 1.0% across all waves, with population counts rising from ~196,600 (2009) to ~243,800 (2018), reflecting demographic growth. People with psychosocial disability were disproportionately middle-aged, Australian-born, socioeconomically disadvantaged and living outside major cities. Under the medium growth scenario, projected counts increase from ~274,000 (2025) to ~410,000 (2060; +50%), with those experiencing profound limitation projected to nearly double (+92%). Shifting from diagnosis- to function-based estimation, this study provides a policy-relevant basis for psychosocial disability planning. Rapid growth in the number of profound psychosocial disability underscores the need for early intervention and coordinated psychosocial supports beyond Australia's National Disability Insurance Scheme.

title: Mapping the prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis in Middle East and North Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence has increased to medium-to-high levels in several countries of the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), while Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) exposure as one of the most consistently reported MS risk factors is common throughout the region. This systematic review and meta-analysis descriptively mapped published estimates of MS prevalence and EBV seroprevalence alongside each other in MENA countries. We searched MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science until 18 June 2022. Observational studies reporting MS prevalence or EBV seroprevalence among healthy MENA populations were eligible. For quantitative EBV synthesis, we restricted analyses to studies reporting VCA-IgG seroprevalence to improve comparability across studies. Studies reporting the prevalence of specific type of MS or those assessing EBV infection by IgA antibodies or non-serological tissues or without a control arm representing general population were excluded. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools were used to determine the quality of the studies. The heterogeneity of studies was evaluated using I2 statistics. Results of the fix-effects meta-analysis were presented using prevalence and 95% confidence intervals. Of 4,323 records identified, 131 studies were included. The pooled MS prevalence was 51.02 per 100,000 population, and the pooled EBV VCA-IgG seroprevalence was 75%. In time-stratified analyses, pooled MS prevalence increased from 12 per 100,000 in studies conducted up to 2000 to 58 per 100,000 in studies conducted from 2011 to 2022. Pooled EBV seroprevalence increased from 71 to 75% across the same periods. These findings suggest that the prevalence of both MS and EBV has increased over time, with a more pronounced increase observed for MS. Between-study heterogeneity was extreme for both outcomes (I2 = 100%), reflecting substantial variation in geography, populations, study methods, diagnostic approaches, and study periods. Published MS prevalence estimates and EBV VCA-IgG seroprevalence estimates showed co-occurring uprising patterns in the available MENA literature. Based on a probable ecological correlation between the increasing prevalence of MS and EBV, the preventive measures against EBV infection may potentially yield favorable outcomes in terms of MS prevention. Future longitudinal, population-based studies with standardized MS ascertainment and age-specific EBV serology are needed.

title: Molecular insights into GPR55 modulation reveal an atypical activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent efficacy regulation.
abstract: GPR55 is a lipid-activated G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) implicated in metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) species are proposed as endogenous agonists, but progress in understanding GPR55 function has still been limited by suboptimal chemical probes. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GPR55 in both inactive and active states. The inactive-state structure bound to the inverse agonist CID16020046 facilitated the rational design of an improved in vitro tool compound, BI-8310. Surprisingly, mutation of a glycosylation site in extracellular loop 2 converted CID16020046 into a potent agonist, enabling co-structure determination of the active, G13-bound receptor. Comparative analysis of both states bound to the same ligand provides insights into an atypical activation mechanism that diverges from the typical helix VI outward movement observed in other GPCRs. Functional mutagenesis, N-glycoproteomics, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) substantiate the findings. These results establish a basis for targeted modulation of GPR55 in pathophysiological conditions.

title: Impact of clinical risk factors on white matter microstructure in preterm-born infants: investigation with diffusion MRI and tractography at term-equivalent age.
abstract: Premature birth occurs during a phase of intense brain maturation, making white matter (WM) particularly vulnerable to injury. Beyond major lesions, subtle and widespread microstructural alterations also contribute to later neurodevelopmental impairments. We aimed to characterize the impact of key clinical risk factors on global and tract-specific WM microstructure at term-equivalent age (TEA), using 3T-diffusion-MRI data of 111 infants born before 33 weeks of gestation. We implemented a tractography pipeline adapted for use in infants with heterogeneous brain anatomy, including macroscopic abnormalities and lesions, and extracted diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics in sensorimotor tracts: corticospinal tract (CST), superior thalamic radiation (STR), frontal aslant tract (FAT), forceps minor (FMI) and middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP). Associations with risk factors were assessed accounting for age at MRI or global WM microstructure. Tractography succeeded in most infants despite marked anatomical variability and/or overt lesions. Being a male, small for gestational age (SGA) at birth, encountering sepsis and having severe Kidokoro radiological score for WM were associated with altered global WM metrics. At the tract level, CST and STR showed the strongest susceptibility to SGA, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and Kidokoro score. In contrast, associations after adjustment for global WM microstructure suggested that FAT might be less vulnerable than other tracts to extreme prematurity, SGA and invasive ventilation. Findings were partially replicated in infants without macroscopic abnormalities, supporting the presence of WM dysmaturation even in the absence of visible injury. DTI metrics thus provide tract-specific biomarkers of early WM microstructure in preterm infants, which are sensitive to risk factors and could inform targeted prevention and intervention.

title: Association of pain intensity and pain extent as assessed by pain drawings with clinical and psychosocial factors in patients with temporomandibular disorders.
abstract: Despite the widespread use of pain drawings in the assessment of temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), clinicians still lack clear evidence for which pain dimensions derived from these tools meaningfully reflect functional disability and psychosocial burden. The purpose of this cross-sectional clinical study was to investigate the relationship between the intensity and extent of pain and various clinical and psychosocial factors in Iranian patients with TMDs. Patients diagnosed with TMDs according to the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD) were recruited from a clinical population. Pain extent was quantified using standardized head and neck pain drawings, while pain intensity was assessed using the Characteristic Pain Intensity (CPI) derived from the Graded Chronic Pain Scale (GCPS). Clinical and psychosocial variables were evaluated using validated questionnaires, including pain-related disability (GCPS), jaw functional limitation (JFLS-8), depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), psychological distress (PHQ-4), somatic symptom burden (PHQ-15), and oral parafunctional behaviors (OBC). Data were analyzed using the Spearman rho, and group comparisons were performed using independent t tests (α=.05). A total of 114 participants aged 18 to 65 years were included. CPI (GCPS) showed a significant positive association with pain-related disability (P=.008), indicating greater functional impairment with increasing CPI (GCPS). In contrast, pain extent was not significantly associated with pain-related disability, jaw functional limitation, or any psychosocial variables (P>.05 for all). No significant differences in CPI (GCPS) or pain extent were observed according to sex (P=.546 and P=.261, respectively) or pain laterality (P=.108 and P=.249, respectively). CPI (GCPS) appeared to be a more clinically meaningful indicator of functional impact than the spatial extent of pain distribution as assessed by head and neck pain drawings in patients with TMDs. Pain drawings should be interpreted as a complementary descriptive tool rather than a standalone marker of disease severity or psychosocial burden, with greater emphasis placed on CPI (GCPS) in clinical assessment.

title: Photobiomodulation in Parkinson's disease: From pathogenesis to intervention.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder clinically characterized by bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Its core pathological features include the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons within the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatal dopamine depletion, and intracellular accumulation of misfolded α-Synuclein (α-Syn)-rich Lewy inclusions that trigger neuronal dysfunction and cell death. Despite substantial research efforts, existing pharmacological strategies targeting α-Syn and dopaminergic neurons show limited capacity to halt or reverse PD progression, creating an urgent need for novel alternative therapeutic interventions. Photobiomodulation (PBM) is a non-invasive phototherapy that delivers photonic energy to biological tissues using visible and near-infrared light. Preclinical studies have documented neuroprotective signals linked to PBM in experimental PD models; however, clinical studies to date provide only preliminary and inconsistent evidence regarding safety and possible symptomatic benefit. This narrative review outlines the mechanistic rationale, preclinical findings, clinical observations, and key translational limitations for PBM as an investigational adjunctive intervention in PD. We first elaborate on PD-related pathological mechanisms, followed by an in-depth discussion of PBM-mediated biological actions, and consolidate recent evidence for its anti-PD applications in preclinical settings. Available preclinical data suggest PBM could modulate mitochondrial function, neuroinflammation, dopaminergic-neuron survival, and responses along the microbiota-gut-brain axis in experimental PD models, though direct evidence supporting modification of α-synuclein aggregation or propagation remains sparse. Clinical observations support procedural feasibility and acceptable short-term safety profiles. Nevertheless, definitive clinical efficacy cannot be confirmed given small sample sizes, heterogeneous intervention protocols, and inconsistent outcomes from controlled trials. PBM should currently be regarded as an investigational adjunctive strategy rather than an established therapy for PD.

title: Integrated multi-omics reveals synaptic vulnerability, mitochondrial impairment, and systemic lipid remodeling as translational hallmarks of postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is a common complication after surgery, but its systemic molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Using a murine model combining 2% isoflurane anesthesia and laparotomy, we integrated spatial proteomics (frontal cortex, hippocampus, and hypothalamus), serum proteomics, and serum lipidomics to elucidate the pathophysiology of POCD. POCD mice showed significant behavioral deficits (reduced open field exploration and impaired Morris water maze performance). Proteomics revealed synaptic dysregulation in the frontal cortex (e.g., Sptan1 upregulation) and mitochondrial dysfunction in the hippocampus (e.g., Ogdh downregulation), along with activated MAPK signaling. Serum lipidomics revealed elevated triglyceride and lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) (22:6) levels and decreased sphingomyelin and ether lipid levels. Integrated pathway analysis revealed neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and proteostasis disruption. These findings demonstrate that POCD arises from synergistic dysregulation of synaptic integrity, systemic lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial function. Key molecules such as Sptan1 and Ogdh and those with altered TG/LPC (22:6) ratios have emerged as candidate molecules associated with POCD, suggesting potential directions for therapeutic intervention.

title: Early-life prolonged hyperthermic seizures alter disease trajectory in the Scn1a(+/-)tm1Kea mouse model of Dravet syndrome.
abstract: Dravet syndrome (DS) is a catastrophic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused most often by de novo loss-of-function mutations in SCN1A, the gene encoding the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav1.1). Animal models such as the Scn1a(+/-)tm1Kea mouse display relevant DS phenotypes including sensitivity to hyperthermia-induced seizures and later-life spontaneous seizures. Elevating the body temperature of immature Scn1a(+/-)tm1Kea mice reliably triggers seizures. Typically, researchers evoke only short-lasting seizures by hyperthermia, whereas febrile seizures in DS patients are often prolonged and complex. This study aimed to characterize a more clinically relevant model of hyperthermia-induced seizures in F1.Scn1a(+/-)tm1kea mice and clarify how this affects epilepsy progression, severity, and associated comorbidities in mice of both sexes. A prolonged febrile event (PFE) was achieved by placing P17 pups in a warmed-air stream inside a chamber, with stepped body temperature raising up to 41 °C followed by holding for 30 min, before cooling body temperature to 37 °C. While the PFE procedure induced prolonged and recurrent seizures, bulk cortical Nav1.1 protein abundance remained unchanged across disease progression (P18, P21 and P90). Post-weaning monitoring up to P90 revealed that PFE-exposed F1.Scn1a(+/-)tm1kea mice displayed higher mortality rates and altered survival patterns, with distinct outcomes observed in male and female mice. As adults, PFE-exposed F1.Scn1a(+/-)tm1kea mice displayed increased locomotor and exploratory behavior, whereas PFE-exposed F1.Scn1a(+/+) mice exhibited impaired spatial reference memory. The findings suggest that early-life prolonged hyperthermia-induced seizures influence multiple disease-related phenotypes in this DS model, some of which may exhibit sex-specific differences. The findings extend the range of tools to study DS and provide insights into how a background of prolonged FS may impact later-life outcomes in mice.

title: Novel variant in KARS1 in a consanguineous family with Intellectual Disability and hearing impairment: WES and in silico protein analysis.
abstract: Intellectual Disability (ID) is a genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that imposes a substantial burden on families, with huge demands on healthcare services. Autosomal recessive forms are particularly prevalent in inbred populations, where rare homozygous variants often remain undiagnosed. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing (WES) has emerged as an effective diagnostic approach for resolving the etiology of unresolved cases. Herein, we report a homozygous missense variant in KARS1, a lysyl-tRNA synthetase (c.989 T > C, p.Leu330Pro), co-segregating with ID and hearing impairments in a consanguineous Arab family from Jordan. We integrated WES and in silico analyses to characterize the variant, including evolutionary, pathogenicity, splicing, stability, and comparative 3D modelling analyses. The variant was located in a highly conserved catalytic domain, and multiple pathogenicity classifiers predicted a deleterious impact. The molecular changes included a potential loss of the alpha helix and alterations to the catalytic/allosteric sites. Splicing analyses predicted disruption of exonic regulatory elements, forming a new enhancer motif and a net increase in exonic splicing enhancers. Additionally, the variant was predicted to be destabilizing, with decreased local interactions, including potential clashes with Glu301. The identified variant can potentially disrupt aminoacylation fidelity, and the impaired protein function may compromise both cytosolic and mitochondrial protein synthesis, leading to defective proteostasis, reduced energy production, and altered synaptic development. Our findings highlight the diagnostic value of trio-based WES and computational analyses in consanguineous populations, expand the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of KARS1-related dysfunctions, and support the inclusion of KARS1 in regional diagnostic panels for ID.

title: Identifying the Optimal Respiratory Muscle Training Intervention for Heart Failure Patients: A Network Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Respiratory muscle training interventions have shown promising results in improving functional capacity, quality of life, and prognosis of heart failure patients. However, the optimal respiratory muscle training intervention for rehabilitation remains unclear. A systematic review and network meta-analysis was conducted by searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library until September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effect of respiratory muscle training interventions on maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP), maximum expiratory pressure (MEP), forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁), six-minute walk test (6MWT), peak oxygen uptake (VO2max), quality of life, and dyspnea. Random-effect network meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled mean differences. Interventions were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). A total of 88 RCTs (5,757 participants) were included. Medium-intensity inspiratory muscle training (IMT) ranked highest for improving MIP (SUCRA: 89.8%). Combined aerobic and resistance exercise was optimal for MEP (SUCRA: 79.3%). Aerobic training showed the greatest benefit for FVC (SUCRA: 94.8%) and FEV₁ (SUCRA: 93.8%). Medium-intensity IMT was most effective for enhancing 6MWT performance (SUCRA: 81.6%). A combination of high-intensity IMT with aerobic training yielded the largest gains in improving VO2max (SUCRA: 74.7%), quality of life (SUCRA: 81.4%), and reducing dyspnea (SUCRA: 89.3%). Respiratory muscle training interventions provide different benefits across key rehabilitation outcomes in heart failure. Accordingly, rehabilitation strategies may be optimized by aligning exercise modalities with patients' rehabilitation needs, preferences, and clinical profiles, rather than adopting a uniform prescription.

title: The evolving role of diamond materials in neuroscience and neuroengineering.
abstract: Diamond-based materials are increasingly investigated in neuroscience and neuroengineering because of their tunable surface chemistry, mechanical robustness, electrochemical stability and photostability. This review compares particulate nanodiamonds (NDs), fluorescent NDs, conductive and nanocrystalline diamond electrodes, and NV-containing diamond sensors across neural sensing, imaging, neurochemical monitoring, neural interfacing, regenerative engineering and experimental therapeutic applications. We examine how synthesis, particle size, purity, aggregation, surface chemistry and defect structure influence application-specific performance, biological interactions, biodistribution and safety. Translational potential is assessed according to the available evidence, systemic exposure, technical maturity, manufacturing requirements and regulatory complexity. Localized diagnostic and neurochemical-sensing applications may offer comparatively plausible near-term pathways because they can reduce dependence on systemic delivery. Implantable neural electrodes and retinal interfaces also avoid some systemic barriers but remain predominantly supported by preclinical evidence. ND-based central nervous system (CNS) drug delivery, glioblastoma treatment, neurodegenerative scaffolds and mammalian quantum-neuronal sensing remain at earlier experimental stages. Key barriers include formulation-dependent biocompatibility, sensitivity in complex tissues, blood-brain barrier delivery, long-term biodistribution and clearance, manufacturing reproducibility, GMP-compatible scale-up and regulatory qualification. Although some of these limitations may be reduced through material and process optimization, comparative validation and stronger long-term safety evidence are still required for clinical translation. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Diamond-based materials are increasingly finding their way into neuroscience and neuroengineering by bridging the gap between advanced nanotechnology and living neural systems. This review highlights the versatility of distinct diamond structures-ranging from detonation nanodiamonds and fluorescent defect centers to conductive boron-doped electrodes-across applications like biosensing, neurochemical monitoring, neural interfacing, and targeted therapy.

title: PPT1-mediated GABAARα1 depalmitoylation maintains inhibitory synaptic homeostasis and cognition.
abstract: GABAA receptors (GABAARs), essential for inhibitory neurotransmission, are palmitoylated proteins and their depalmitoylation is catalyzed by palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1). By generating Gabra1em1 knock-in mice carrying mutations that disrupt the interaction between GABAARα1 and PPT1, we found that the mutant mice exhibited impaired learning and memory, whereas the underlying cellular mechanisms remained largely unclear. Molecular analyses showed that heterozygous (HET) Gabra1em1 mice (Gabra1em1HET) displayed normal GABAARα1 protein expression but persistent hyperpalmitoylation of GABAARα1. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated the decreased neuronal excitability, enhanced inhibitory synaptic transmission and impaired hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP). Behavioral analyses further revealed deficits in learning, memory and social behavior. The homozygous (HOMO) Gabra1em1 mice (Gabra1em1HOMO) exhibited a marked reduction in GABAARα1 protein expression, accompanied by enhanced neuronal excitability and excitatory synaptic transmission, but impaired LTP and learning and memory along with a shorten life span. Collectively, these findings indicate that Gabra1em1 HET mice represent a valuable model for investigating the physiological and pathological roles of protein palmitoylation, as aberrant GABAARα1 palmitoylation disrupts neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and cognitive function without altering receptor expression. In contrast, the phenotypes observed in Gabra1em1 HOMO mice are primarily attributable to the marked reduction in GABAARα1 protein expression, which consequently impairs synaptic plasticity and learning and memory. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into the role of protein palmitoylation in neurological disorders and offer a theoretical foundation for the development of precision therapeutic strategies targeting palmitoylation homeostasis.

title: CSF1R haploinsufficiency reveals subtle and selective age- and sex-dependent vulnerabilities in cognition and white matter without overt neurodegeneration.
abstract: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R), yet the extent to which CSF1R haploinsufficiency alone drives cognitive and neurobiological dysfunction remains unclear. Here, we performed a longitudinal multi-level characterization of behavioral, neuroimaging, cellular, and molecular phenotypes in male and female Csf1r+/- mice to determine the impact of partial CSF1R loss across aging. Cognitive function was assessed using touchscreen-based tasks probing cognitive flexibility, working memory, selective attention, and extinction learning, given that executive function is mainly compromised in ALSP. Brain microstructure was evaluated by diffusion-weighted MRI, complemented by MALDI mass spectrometry imaging to examine regional phospholipid composition. Cell-type quantification and gene expression analyses were performed to identify potential cellular and molecular correlates. Across most domains and ages, Csf1r+/- mice exhibited preserved cognitive performance and cellular composition. Within this broadly intact framework, subtle, age- and sex-dependent vulnerabilities emerged. Aged females showed reduced fractional anisotropy and neurite density in the corpus callosum and left primary motor cortex, along with region-specific alterations in phosphatidylcholine species. Aged males exhibited increased response persistence at the final extinction session and elevated false alarm rates under maximal attentional load. Notably, these changes occurred in the absence of microglial or oligodendrocyte loss, indicating mild microstructural and circuit-level alterations rather than widespread neurodegeneration. Collectively, these findings indicate that CSF1R haploinsufficiency does not recapitulate the severe phenotype of ALSP but instead reveals selective, sex-specific vulnerabilities in white matter and cognitive function. This profile is consistent with a sensitized state in which additional factors may be required to drive disease progression.

title: Common Phenomenal and Neural Substrate Geometry in Visual Motion Perception.
abstract: What is a possible physical substrate of the qualitative aspects of consciousness (qualia)? Answering this question is a central goal of consciousness research. Due to their subjective and ineffable nature, finding a quantitative way to characterise qualia from verbal description has thus far proven elusive. To overcome the challenge of expressing subjective experience, recent structural and relational approaches have been proposed from mathematics. Yet, as far as we know, no attempts have been made to evaluate the relationship between a certain structure of qualia and the structure of a candidate underlying physical substrate. Towards this ambitious goal of linking the structures of qualia and physical, we set out to make an empirical first step by focusing on experienced dissimilarity of visual motion in human participants and stimulus-evoked neural population response geometry recorded from mouse primary visual cortex. From human participants (N=171), we obtained dissimilarity ratings of visual motion experiences induced by 48 stimuli, spanning across 8 directions and 6 spatial frequencies. Analysis revealed a human dissimilarity structure that was not well captured by a simple monotonic function of physical motion-direction difference alone nor by a pure orientation-symmetry account. From nine individual mice, we recorded single-neuron activity (n=751) with optical imaging in both awake and lightly anaesthetised conditions (isoflurane 0.6-0.8%). From neuron population responses to a similar set of motion stimuli, we computed a distance matrix that is comparable to our human dissimilarity matrix. Quantitative analyses show structural commonalities between a human dissimilarity structure and mouse neural structure, where a categorical organisation of stimulus direction best explained both. These commonalities were similar in awake and anaesthetised recordings, suggesting that this coarse V1 geometry is relatively insensitive to this type of anaesthesia; future work combining behaviour with causal intervention is required to relate such neural structures to conscious experience. Finally, we list several empirical factors that can be improved to promote our qualia structure approach in the future.

title: Temporal trends of treatment and mortality in small renal masses <2cm.
abstract: To explore contemporary rates and temporal trends of Guidelines-recommended management options for small renal masses (SRM)<2cm, that include non-interventional management (NIM), local tumor destruction (LTD) and nephrectomy (either partial -PN- or radical -RN). Within the SEER database (2004-2022), SRM<2cm patients were identified and stratified according to four examined management options. Estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) were tabulated according to management type. Five-years cancer-specific mortality (CSM) rates were computed. Multivariable logistic regression tested predictors of NIM, LTD and RN. Of 20,769 SRM<2cm patients, 12,107 (58.3%) underwent PN vs. 3,558 (17.1%) NIM vs. 2,879 (13.9%) RN vs. 2,225 (10.7%) LTD. During the study span, NIM rates increased from 8.0% in 2004 to 23.9% in 2022 (EAPC+5.1%, p<0.001). The increase in NIM rates was more pronounced in patients aged ≥70 years (from 22.0% to 45.9%, ∆+23.9, EAPC +3.3%, p<0.001). and in African American (from 4.5% to 23.2%, ∆+18.7, EAPC +5.0%, p<0.001). At multivariable logistic regression models age ≥70 years (OR 9.24, p<0.001) and African American race (OR 1.39, p<0.001) independently predicted NIM. Five-years CSM remained stable over the study span: 2.8% in 2004 and 2.9% in 2017 (EAPC -1.0%, p=0.4). In SRM<2cm patients, rates of NIM are very low, even in the most recent study years. However, NIM rates increased overtime across all sex, age and race categories, with most pronounced increase among elderly and African American. Concurrently, five-years CSM rates have not increased despite the wider adoption of NIM.

title: Autophagy in Ocular Health and Disease: From Mechanistic Insights to Therapeutic Perspectives.
abstract: Autophagy represents a lysosomal degradative pathway through which cells systematically break down and recycle their own constituents, including proteins, lipid droplets, and entire organelles, by sequestering them within double-membrane autophagosomes prior to lysosomal fusion. Beyond its role as a fundamental quality control mechanism, this process critically shapes cellular metabolism and preserves intracellular equilibrium. In ocular biology, autophagic activity is involved in structural morphogenesis during eye development and becomes dysregulated across a spectrum of vision-threatening disorders. This review synthesises current evidence on autophagy throughout distinct ocular compartments, with particular attention given to its pathogenic contributions to corneal disease, cataract formation, glaucomatous neurodegeneration, and major retinopathies, with the goal of advancing the understanding of the underlying mechanism in this evolving field.

title: Diffusion MRI reveals stage-dependent microstructural responses to early ferroptosis inhibition in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
abstract: Neurodegeneration drives irreversible disability in multiple sclerosis (MS). Ferroptosis has been implicated in MS and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), but its spatiotemporal dynamics and imaging correlates remain unclear. We combined 7.0 T diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) with histopathological and molecular analyses to evaluate the effects of Liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1) in mice with EAE induced by myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein peptide 35-55 (MOG35-55). Sixty-four female C57BL/6 mice were assigned to control, EAE, early-treatment (Early-Tx; Lip-1 from day 12), and late-treatment (Late-Tx; Lip-1 from day 18) groups. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and tissue analyses were performed at days 20 and 30 post-immunization. Early-Tx reduced clinical severity at day 30 (vs. EAE; p < 0.001) and limited body weight loss. At peak disease, voxel- and ROI-based DTI showed increased mean diffusivity and radial diffusivity in the corpus callosum, internal capsule, and thalamus, which were attenuated by Early-Tx. At the chronic stage, EAE showed persistent fractional anisotropy reduction in periventricular white matter and corpus callosum, whereas Early-Tx largely prevented these abnormalities. Histology demonstrated that Early-Tx suppressed inflammatory infiltration, microglial activation, and demyelination while preserving myelin integrity. Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) upregulation and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) downregulation preceded overt iron deposition, whereas iron accumulation emerged mainly at the chronic stage and colocalized with activated microglia and demyelinated lesions. Ferroptosis-related molecular alterations are associated with stage-dependent inflammatory demyelinating injury in EAE. Early Lip-1 treatment provides greater microstructural protection than delayed treatment. High-field DTI sensitively detects treatment-responsive microstructural injury and may help monitor ferroptosis-related pathology in demyelinating disease.

title: Multimodal evidence associated with 20Hz rTMS in AD: neuroaxonal injury reduction, neural oscillatory rebalancing, and multilayer network integration.
abstract: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been demonstrated to enhance cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neurobiological mechanisms associated with neuroaxonal injury, neural oscillatory dynamics, and large-scale network reorganization remain unclear. In this study, we first conducted a randomized, sham-controlled trial with 16 patients with AD to evaluate the efficacy of DLPFC-targeted rTMS, followed by a single-arm multimodal cohort study of 30 patients to explore potential neurobiological mechanisms through cognitive assessments, blood biomarkers, EEG oscillatory activity, and multiplex brain network analysis. In Stage 1, the sham group showed no significant pre-post changes in MMSE or MoCA scores (MMSE: Z = -0.738, Cohen's r = 0.26; MoCA: Z =-0.853, Cohen's r = 0.30). The active rTMS group showed improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.124, Cohen's r = 0.75) and MoCA (Z = -2.108, Cohen's r = 0.75). In stage 2, rTMS was associated with improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.863, Cohen's r = 0.523) and MoCA (t = -6.137, Cohen's r = 0.752) scores. Biomarker analyses indicated a significant decrease in NfL concentrations (Z=-2.371, Cohen's r=0.484). EEG recordings revealed a decrease in delta power in the left temporal lobe (t=2.158, Cohen's r=0.372) and increases in beta power in the right parietal lobe and gamma power in the temporal lobe (beta: Z=-2.088, Cohen's r=0.381; gamma: Z=-2.129, Cohen's r=0.389). Network analysis showed reduced modularity and enhanced global efficiency across theta, alpha, and beta bands, accompanied by increased degree of overlap in frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Importantly, MoCA improvement correlated with gamma-band global efficiency (R=0.389, P=0.034) and multilayer clustering coefficients in the left frontal and right occipital regions (R=0.478, P=0.008; R=0.398, P=0.029). Overall, rTMS exposure was associated with cognitive improvements in patients with AD, together with changes in neurodegeneration-related biomarkers and EEG network organization. These findings suggest that cognitive changes following rTMS may be associated with oscillatory modulation and large-scale network remodeling. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Registration number: ChiCTR2500095949; Registration Date: 2025-01-15.

title: Cascade liposomal delivery for glioblastoma through multi-stage biological checkpoints.
abstract: Although receptor-targeted liposomes provide promising opportunities for glioblastoma therapy, their clinical translation remains limited by sequential biological barriers encountered after systemic administration. Here, we establish a multi-stage checkpoint framework linking carrier properties with stage-specific transport constraints, including systemic clearance, BBB/BTB heterogeneity, extracellular matrix resistance, and myeloid sequestration. We analyze receptor-mediated transcytosis through a mechanistic triad of ligand engagement, intracellular sorting, and abluminal release, highlighting the binding-site barrier and affinity paradox that restrict effective parenchymal delivery. Successful transcytosis represents only the initial step and we further develop a cascade targeting framework integrating tissue penetration, tumor cell recognition, and intracellular payload availability. Key translational challenges, including tumor microenvironment modulation, Quality by Design (QbD) manufacturing, safety, and companion diagnostics, are critically examined. Future progress will depend on evaluating liposomal platforms according to productive cellular exposure, with bulk accumulation serving only as a supporting measure, and on using quantitative transport profiling and imaging-guided stratification to identify patients whose biological barriers are compatible with specific liposomal designs.

title: Intraoperative and postoperative fluid administration is associated with transfusion in open arteriovenous malformation and aneurysm surgery.
journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
abstract: Red blood cell transfusion to manage hemodynamic instability or blood loss during and after open cerebrovascular surgery has been associated with postoperative complications, making transfusion avoidance an important quality-improvement target. Iatrogenic hemodilution from liberal crystalloid administration may contribute to perioperative anemia, but its relevance in open aneurysm and arteriovenous malformation (AVM) surgery is poorly defined. We investigated factors associated with receiving intraoperative and postoperative transfusion in these open cerebrovascular procedures and the association between transfusion and early postoperative outcomes. In this single-center retrospective propensity-matched cohort study, patients who underwent open aneurysm or AVM surgery and received an intraoperative or postoperative red blood cell transfusion were matched 1:1 with non-transfused controls. Perioperative variables-including intraoperative and 72-h postoperative fluid administration, estimated blood loss, physiological parameters, comorbidities, and laboratory values-were compared using univariate analysis, and multivariable Firth logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with transfusion. To address the temporal relationship between fluid and transfusion, a time-anchored analysis compared pre-transfusion fluids received with fluids received by controls to the same time point. Intensive care unit and hospital length of stay were evaluated. Fifty-six patients (28 transfused, 28 controls) were analyzed. Transfused patients received more intravenous fluid in the first 72 postoperative hours (13.1 ± 4.4 vs 9.8 ± 4.6 L, p = 0.009), and transfusion percentage increased across fluid quartiles (21 %, 50 %, 64 %, and 64 %; p for trend = 0.020). Transfused patients also had a higher American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class and longer operative duration. Similarly, in the time-anchored analysis, receiving more fluids was associated with transfusion (adjusted OR 1.28 per L, 95 % CI 1.14-1.45), including after additional adjustment for ASA class (OR 1.23, 95 % CI 1.08-1.40). Intensive care unit and hospital stays were longer among transfused patients, but the differences were not statistically significant. Greater fluid administration perioperatively was associated with receiving intraoperative or postoperative transfusion after open aneurysm and AVM surgery. These findings are consistent with, but do not establish, a contribution of iatrogenic hemodilution, and they support prospective evaluation of fluid management.

title: Pain mechanisms in trigeminal neuralgia: From peripheral pathology to brain network reorganization and neurosurgical implications.
journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
abstract: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) involves peripheral neurovascular pathology and may also be associated with maladaptive neuroplastic changes in central nervous system networks. This review synthesizes evidence on peripheral and central pain mechanisms, neuroimaging biomarkers, molecular and transcriptomic correlates, and neurosurgical implications, including emerging neuromodulation strategies. This narrative review drew on topic-oriented searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science conducted between June 27 and July 5, 2026, covering literature published through June 2026. Supplementary targeted searches and reference-list screening were used to identify relevant publications. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively. Evidence supports a multilevel model of TN involving peripheral pathology and central neuroplastic changes. Neuroimaging studies report structural and functional alterations in sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and default mode networks, alongside disrupted structure-function coupling. Partial restoration of functional connectivity after neurosurgical treatment has been reported, although outcomes vary. Transcriptomic findings link imaging abnormalities to genes involved in ion channel function, synaptic signaling, neuroinflammation, and energy metabolism but remain hypothesis-generating. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may provide short-term analgesic benefit; however, evidence is limited and heterogeneous. TN may be understood as a disorder involving interactions between peripheral pathology and central nervous system reorganization. Integrating neuroimaging and molecular evidence may inform future patient stratification and neurosurgical decision-making. Individualized neuromodulation remains investigational and requires further clinical validation.

title: Temporal evolution of EEG hallmarks in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
abstract: The temporal development of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) and slow spike-and-wave complexes in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) remains poorly characterized. This study mapped the emergence and longitudinal evolution of these EEG hallmarks in a real-world LGS cohort. This retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric neurophysiology and neurology center. Patients aged 1-18 years fulfilling current International League Against Epilepsy criteria for LGS were identified through local databases. All available sleep video-EEG recordings before November 2024 were reviewed; clinical features, EEG findings, and comorbidities were collected at each recording. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. We reviewed 234 EEGs from 51 patients (75% male). Median age at first EEG was 5 years. GPFA emerged later than slow spike-and-wave (mean age: 9.6 vs 8.3 years, p = 0.002), with non-parametric analysis confirming a significant difference in age at first detection (p = 0.004). Median age at epilepsy onset was 1.1 years, while all clinical and EEG criteria for LGS were met at a median age of 10.9 years. EEG hallmarks of LGS emerged progressively during childhood, with slow spike-and-wave preceding GPFA during sleep. Following early clinical manifestations, a prolonged developmental phase may precede full electroclinical expression of LGS, with implications for early diagnosis and longitudinal EEG surveillance.

title: Influence of the treatment protocol on the dental arch width and occlusal characteristics of 6-year-old patients with cleft lip and/or palate.
journal: Journal of cranio-maxillo-facial surgery : official publication of the European Association for Cranio-Maxillo-Facial Surgery
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the maxillary width and occlusal characteristics of six-year-old patients with cleft lip and/or palate treated with two different surgical protocols. Six-year-old patients with cleft palate (CP), unilateral cleft lip and palate (UCLP), and bilateral cleft lip and palate (BCLP) treated with protocol A (soft palate closure at 1 year using a modified Veau-Wardill-Kilner pushback technique, and hard palate closure between 5 and 7 years using the von Langenbeck procedure) or protocol B (soft palate closure at 1 year using Sommerlad intravelar veloplasty, and hard palate closure with a vomer flap at the time of lip repair) were included. A non-cleft control group was used for comparison. Maxillary and mandibular arch width, maxillary arch length, dental arch relationship, sagittal molar occlusion, overjet, overbite, and crossbite prevalence were assessed. Groups were compared using non-parametric tests and proportional odds models. In total, 134 patients (58 CP, 51 UCLP, and 25 BCLP) were included: 79 treated with protocol A and 55 with protocol B. Eighty-one controls were included. No statistically significant differences were observed between the two protocols for most outcomes, although protocol B required fewer treatment interventions.

title: Visual-linguistic cues in manual communication: Neural and behavioral responses to Mouthings in sign-naïve perception.
abstract: Gesture serves as a foundational modality for conveying event structure, providing critical visual information about transitivity and participant roles. Sign languages integrate manual (hand-based) and non-manual (face, torso, head) articulations to encode complex linguistic information. Among these, mouth movements provide phonological and lexical cues, but their role in sign-naïve individuals remains underexplored. This study investigates how sign-naïve individuals process non-manual markers (mouthings) in unfamiliar signed verbs, to explore how linguistic information is extracted from visual stimuli sharing properties with both gesture and sign language. Using EEG, we examined whether lip-reading functions as a linguistic cue or a general perceptual enhancement in non-signers viewing Austrian Sign Language (ÖGS) and non-ÖGS stimuli. Findings reveal distinct neural signatures for manual signs presented with and without congruent mouthings. An early posterior negativity followed by a late posterior positivity suggests that mouthings facilitate lexical access by providing phonological cues that activate stored lexical representations. Conversely, stimuli without mouthings elicited increased anterior activity, reflecting heightened cognitive control demands. Further, telic verbs, which inherently encode event endpoints, showed earlier and stronger facilitation from congruent mouthings compared to atelic verbs. These findings align with the Event Visibility Hypothesis and reinforce the role of visual cues in linguistic comprehension.

title: Aniline-linked coumarin-triazole hybrids as α-glucosidase inhibitors: An insightful study from synthesis to in vivo efficacy and mechanistic analysis.
abstract: A new series of coumarin-aniline-triazole hybrids 12a-p was prepared using a multi-step approach. This synthesis involved a Knoevenagel condensation between 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde and diethyl malonate, followed by ester hydrolysis and amide coupling to yield a coumarin-based alkyne, which was then reacted with various 2-azido-N-arylacetamides via a click reaction. All synthesized compounds were evaluated for their potential antidiabetic activities through α-glucosidase inhibition, possessing remarkably superior potency compared to the reference drug acarbose (IC50 = 750.0 ± 0.8 μM), with IC50 values ranging from 1.1 to 44.2 μM. Among them, the 2-methyl derivative 12b emerged as the most potent, exhibiting approximately 750-fold greater activity than acarbose. Kinetic studies established that 12b was a competitive inhibitor (Kᵢ = 1700 nM), and selectivity assays confirmed its excellent specificity for α-glucosidase over α-amylase (no activity was observed up to 100 μM), suggesting a reduced risk of gastrointestinal side effects. Spectral investigations using circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy revealed that 12b induced significant conformational rearrangements in the enzyme, characterized by a noticeable increase in β-sheet content (from 32.3% to 81.3%), while fluorescence spectroscopy confirmed a 1:1 binding stoichiometry with high affinity (Ka = 1.75 × 105 L mol-1 at 25 °C) and an enthalpy-driven binding mechanism (ΔH = -39.19 kJ mol-1, ΔS = -31.07 J mol-1 K-1). In vivo studies in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model demonstrated that, while compound 12b at 30 mg/kg exhibited significant antihyperglycemic activity (55% reduction in FBG), its efficacy was slightly lower than that of acarbose (62% reduction in FBG). Additionally, histopathological examination confirmed dose-dependent protective effects against diabetes-induced hepatic and pancreatic damage. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations also provided structural insights into the stable binding of 12b within the α-glucosidase active site (with a mean binding energy of -10.02 kcal/mol), establishing persistent hydrogen-bonding interactions with key residues, particularly ARG439 and LYS155. Collectively, these findings represent compound 12b as a promising lead candidate for further optimization and development as a safe and effective α-glucosidase inhibitor for the management of type 2 diabetes.

title: Schaftoside from galgeuntang as a multi-target class I histone deacetylase inhibitor: Integrated molecular docking, dynamics, and systems pharmacology analysis.
abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are enzymes that remove acetyl groups from lysine residues of histone proteins, playing a critical role in gene expression regulation. Particularly, Class I HDACs (HDAC1, HDAC2, and HDAC8) are implicated in cancer development and have attracted significant interest as therapeutic targets. However, developing isoform-selective HDAC inhibitors remains challenging. We screened 1625 phytocompounds from the Korean herbal formulation Galgeuntang using the Traditional Chinese Medicine Systems Pharmacology database. After applying drug-likeness filtering, 235 compounds underwent molecular docking against HDAC1, HDAC2, and HDAC8. Schaftoside emerged as the sole candidate engaging all three isoforms, with binding energies of -115.1, -103.8, and -135.5 kcal/mol, respectively. ADMET profiling, quantitative cytotoxicity predictions across multiple cancer cell lines, and in silico gene expression analysis were then performed. One hundred nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations confirmed stable complex formation and PCA-based free energy landscape analysis revealed well-defined conformational minima for each complex. Schaftoside exhibited potent predicted cytotoxicity against hematological and gastrointestinal malignancies (selectivity Index: 8.7-18.6), including the cisplatin-resistant A2780cisR ovarian carcinoma line. In silico transcriptomic profiling predicted downregulation of oncogenic drivers (MYC, STAT3, AKT1) with concurrent upregulation of tumor suppressors (TP53, CDKN1A) and suppression of the HDAC machinery itself. ADMET profiling revealed high aqueous solubility but limited membrane permeability, indicating that structural optimization will be required. Schaftoside therefore constitutes a promising multi-target Class I HDAC inhibitor scaffold, warranting experimental validation through enzymatic assays, histone acetylation analysis, and cell-based cytotoxicity testing.

title: Mapping cardiometabolic risk in Cleveland's urban environment: A participatory systems analysis of place-based drivers and the role of Community Health Workers.
abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) diseases are shaped by place-based social and environmental conditions, yet the dynamic mechanisms linking structural inequities, neighborhood environments, and healthcare systems remain insufficiently understood. This study employed a participatory system dynamics approach, using Group Model Building (GMB), to examine how spatial, social, and institutional processes interact to shape cardiometabolic risk among low-income African American residents in Cleveland, Ohio, and to explore the role of Community Health Workers (CHWs). A community-engaged Group Model Building process engaged residents, Community Health Workers, healthcare providers, public health practitioners, organizational leaders, and academic partners to co-develop a stakeholder-informed causal loop diagram. Across two Group Model Building workshops conducted on November 18, 2023, and February 17, 2024, participants identified drivers of CKM risk and co-developed a stakeholder-informed system map using structured Group Model Building scripts and qualitative workshop data. The systems map depicts CKM risk as emerging from interactions among economic inequality, neighborhood disinvestment, food access, environmental exposures, healthcare fragmentation, screening access, treatment uptake, and disease management. Stakeholders highlighted upstream forces shaping spatial patterns of disadvantage, chronic stress, and healthcare access, contributing to delayed detection and management of risk factors. Three reinforcing dynamics were identified: (1) a limit-to-success dynamic constraining CHW capacity due to insufficient reimbursement; (2) a shifting-the-burden dynamic emphasizing individual responses over structural reform; and (3) a success-to-the-successful dynamic favoring biomedical care over community-based prevention. These findings suggest how cardiometabolic inequities are sustained through interconnected feedback loops and highlight leverage points-including sustainable CHW financing, cross-sector coordination, and neighborhood investment-to inform place-based strategies to reduce inequities.

title: Discovery of a fluorinated benzoxathiazine AMPA receptor PAM that stabilizes the GluA2 dimer interface and displays antidepressant-like effects.
abstract: Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors hold significant therapeutic promise for neuropsychiatric disorders driven by synaptic dysfunction. Building upon our previously established oxathiazine-dioxide scaffold, we designed and synthesized a novel series of compounds through systematic exploration of the 6-position. Among these compounds, the fluorinated analog C17 was identified as a superior lead candidate. Advanced Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulations demonstrated that C17 stabilizes the GluA2 ligand-binding domain (LBD) dimer more effectively than the clinical benchmark TAK-653. By establishing a robust hydrogen-bonding network, C17 acts as a "molecular glue" to tightly lock the receptor in its canonical activated conformation, thereby preventing transition into the desensitized state. Translating these mechanistic insights into in vivo activity, C17 exhibited potent antidepressant-like efficacy in a chronic social defeat stress mouse model. Electrophysiological characterization confirmed that C17 potentiates (S)-AMPA-induced currents in rat hippocampal neurons without intrinsic agonism. Furthermore, C17 concentration-dependently upregulated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. These results identify C17 as an AMPA receptor PAM with a distinct dimer-stabilizing profile, positioning it as a compelling candidate for treating major depressive disorder (MDD).

title: Assessing physicians' knowledge, attitudes, beliefs, and guideline adherence in the management of low back pain: A multidimensional evaluation.
abstract: This study explored physicians' ability to suspect/identify specific low back pain (LBP); assess their knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs regarding non-specific LBP and self-reported knowledge of LBP guidelines; and identify physician-related factors associated with both specific and non-specific LBP management. This cross-sectional study targeted first-line care physicians. A vignette depicting lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) assessed the ability to suspect/identify a specific underlying cause of LBP, while the Rainville-vignette evaluated whether non-specific LBP management is guideline-consistent. Knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs were assessed using the Back Pain Attitudes Questionnaire (Back-PAQ), Health Care Provider's Pain and Impairment Relationship Scale (HC-PAIRS), and Neurophysiology of Pain Questionnaire. Physicians self-reported their guideline knowledge. Of 100 physicians, 42 correctly mentioned LSS; 31 did so without considering other neurological or vascular causes. Eighty-two percent and 36% gave guideline-consistent recommendations for activity and work. Physicians with helpful Back-PAQ scores had higher odds (OR: 3.23) of providing guideline-consistent activity recommendations, while those with unhelpful HC-PAIRS outcomes had lower odds (OR: 0.47). Yet, 56% viewed the spine as generally vulnerable, and 94% agreed that LBP leaves a lasting weakness. Managing LBP in first-line care remains challenging. The ability to identify specific LBP was limited and the analyses provided no clear evidence of associations with guideline knowledge or the other examined factors. Unhelpful beliefs about spinal vulnerability were also observed alongside guideline-consistent activity advice. These findings should not be interpreted as causal and point to a need for qualitative research when investigating clinical decision-making to inform targeted educational interventions.

title: Operative challenges and functional outcomes of salvage microsurgery in Gamma Knife-failed vestibular schwannoma: A 12-year institutional experience.
abstract: Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is a benign tumor of the vestibular nerve. In selected cases, Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) is used due to its minimally invasive nature and reported tumor control rates of approximately 90%. Salvage microsurgery after failed GKRS is uncommon, and its technical difficulty remains debated. Some authors report increased surgical challenges, while others find no significant differences compared to primary microsurgery. This study presents our experience with salvage microsurgery for VS following failed GKRS, focusing on operative challenges and outcomes. This retrospective observational study was conducted at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), India. Between 2012 and 2023, 1633 patients underwent surgery for vestibular schwannoma, including primary and recurrent cases. Among these, 24 patients had previously received GKRS and subsequently required salvage microsurgery. We retrieved clinical, radiological, and operative data from institutional medical records and PACS imaging. GKRS parameters, including tumor volume and radiation dose, were obtained from the GKRS department. Of the 24 patients, eight were operated on for right-sided tumors, and sixteen for left-sided tumors. The mean tumor volume increased from 7.8 cc before GKRS to 19.13 cc at surgery. The median interval from symptom onset to GKRS was 28.91 months, while the median duration from GKRS to surgery was 28.81 months. Central contrast enhancement decreased at six months post-GKRS in 66.7% of cases. The mean operative time was 332.92 min, and the mean blood loss was 570 mL. Tumors were firm in 58.3% of cases and moderately vascular in 75%. The fifth and seventh cranial nerves were identified in 62.5% and 75.0% of cases, respectively. Tumor adherence to the brainstem was observed in 17 cases, while significant arachnoid thickening was present in only four cases. Salvage microsurgery after failed Gamma Knife radiosurgery for vestibular schwannoma is feasible and safe. However, post-radiosurgical tissue changes, such as adherence of the cranial nerves to the tumor and difficulty identifying the cranial nerves, make it technically more demanding than primary microsurgery, resulting in lower rates of gross total resection and a higher incidence of facial nerve morbidity. In this setting, a strategy prioritising maximal safe resection and functional preservation, rather than complete tumour clearance, is recommended.

title: Dopamine depletion induces low frequency beta oscillations through a minimal loop in basal ganglia: A computational study.
journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
abstract: Pathological β-band oscillations in the cortex and basal ganglia (BG) are a core electrophysiological hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the precise circuits and temporal dynamics governing their emergence remain incompletely understood. To address this, we developed a computational model of the chronically dopamine-depleted BG and identified a minimal inhibitory microcircuit as a primary generator of network wide β oscillations, which is composed of D2-medium spiny neurons (D2-MSN), fast spiking interneurons (FSI), and prototypic external globus pallidus neurons (GPe-TI). By simulating progressive dopamine loss, we show that distinct synaptic pathways within this loop are engaged in a stage-dependent manner: FSI → D2-MSN projection dominates during early to mid depletion stages, whereas GPe-TI → FSI inhibition prevails in later phases. This temporal shift is accompanied by a progressive slowing of the peak oscillation frequency from 11-13 Hz oscillation to 9-11 Hz oscillation. Overall, our results provide a dynamic, circuit level account for how pathological β rhythms evolve over the course of dopamine depletion, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding stage specific pathophysiology in PD and a novel paradigm for designing adaptive neuromodulation strategies.

title: Fear conditioning research through the lens of meta-analyses: A systematic methodological review.
abstract: Meta-analyses have become foundational tools for evidence synthesis and are receiving increasing attention across research disciplines, including fear conditioning - a central paradigm in affective, behavioral, and clinical neuroscience and psychology - where the number of meta-analyses has notably increased in recent years. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity among these meta-analyses complicates their interpretation and comparability. This review systematically summarizes existing meta-analyses in fear conditioning (n = 26), with particular emphasis on methodological choices and reporting standards. Our findings indicate substantial variability in reporting practices, particularly regarding review processes, applied methodological models, and the operationalization of certain variables, which may challenge reproducibility and interpretability. Most meta-analyses used aggregate data and random-effects models, while moderator analyses were frequently conducted but yielded few significant moderators. Outcome measures were frequently aggregated (e.g., skin conductance, startle responses, ratings) without a clear theoretical rationale. We discuss the implications of moderator analyses, the limited attention to temporal dynamics, and the aggregation of diverse outcome measures. We argue that the field would benefit from more precise reporting, theory-driven analytical decisions, and increased data sharing at both the primary and meta-analytic levels. Such improvements would facilitate individual participant data meta-analyses, which preserve within-study variability, enhance moderator analyses, and address challenges inherent to aggregate-level data synthesis. Establishing and expanding shared infrastructures represents a necessary step toward cumulative, reproducible, and clinically informative work in the future.

title: Impact of newly diagnosed multiple sclerosis on marital status and partner relationship.
abstract: Evidence on short-term impact of multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis on intimate relationships remains limited. This study investigated the perceived impact of MS diagnosis on relationship status within the first year following diagnosis. This survey-based observational study used data from the Swiss Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSR). Factors potentially associated with perceived MS direct impact on relationship status within the first year after diagnosis were explored using logistic regression. Among participants reporting that MS impacted their relationship, we explored changes in relationship status and factors associated with relationship dissolution. Among 881 participants included (74% female), 453 were married, 235 with a partner, and 193 single at diagnosis. Overall, 89 participants (10.1%) reported that MS diagnosis impacted their relationship (i.e., 6.2% of married; 14.5% of partnered; 14% of single). Compared with married participants, partnered (ORadj 2.3; 95%CI 1.30-4.06) and single participants (ORadj 2.26; 95%CI 1.25-4.07) were more likely to report impact. Cognitive symptoms were associated with higher odds of reporting impact (ORadj 2.02, 95%CI 1.28-3.19). Among married participants, primary progressive MS was associated with increased odds of relationship impact (ORadj 3.21; 95%CI 1.15-8.33). Among partnered participants, men were more likely than women to report an impacted relationship (ORadj 3.00; 95%CI 1.23-7.25). Among participants with reported relationship impact, relationship trajectories included continuation, strengthening, and dissolution. None of the studied factors were associated with relationship dissolution. One in ten participants reported MS diagnosis impacting their relationship, and consequent relationship changes were heterogeneous, suggesting that this influence may belong to broader psychosocial processes.

title: Family planning in multiple sclerosis: An Australian perspective.
abstract: To develop evidence-based, Australia-specific recommendations for managing multiple sclerosis (MS) before conception, during pregnancy and after birth, balancing maternal health, disease control, and fetal safety. A panel of seven Australian MS specialists, from academic and clinical backgrounds, convened (April-October 2025) via virtual meetings and email correspondence. A targeted literature review covered MS, pregnancy, postpartum relapse, breastfeeding, vaccination and disease-modifying therapy safety. Guidance from the Therapeutic Goods Administration, international clinical guidelines, and safety data were examined to inform interpretation. Evidence indicates that MS does not increase adverse pregnancy outcomes, although a higher risk of small-for-gestational-age birth may occur. Treatment selection should account for teratogenicity and rebound risk. Teriflunomide, fingolimod, siponimod and cladribine require cessation well before conception and are contraindicated during breastfeeding. Natalizumab can be continued until conception and through the first and second trimesters using extended-interval dosing; postpartum resumption is advised to minimise rebound relapses. Ofatumumab and ocrelizumab should be stopped if pregnancy is confirmed. Treatment decisions should be individualised through shared decision-making. European Union guidance supports use of ocrelizumab during breastfeeding, consistent with evidence of minimal monoclonal antibody transfer into breastmilk. As breastfeeding does not prevent relapse, early postpartum DMT resumption is recommended to reduce relapse risk. Contraceptive use remains low despite requirements for many therapies. With proactive planning, women with MS can achieve optimal pregnancy outcomes. This consensus integrates evidence, regulatory considerations and Australian guidance to support a practical framework for family planning in MS.

title: Amygdala: Function and neural basis.
abstract: This review summarizes our current understanding of the amygdala. As an important part of the limbic system, the amygdala is highly sensitive to environmental stimuli such as sounds. Although the responses of amygdala neurons to sounds are usually not as robust as those of neurons in the primary auditory cortex, the lowest response thresholds of these neurons are consistent with the behavioral audiogram. When a threat is detected through sensory information processing, it immediately triggers a fight-or-flight response, such as freezing and heart rate increase. By learning and remembering environmental events (especially those that may cause harm) and its effects on various instinctive behaviors (such as sexual impulse and maternal behaviors) as well as emotional expressions (such as fear and aggression), it plays a crucial role in the survival and continuation of the species. The response of amygdala neurons to environmental sounds is often composed of an early sharp response component and a late slow response component. The early response is responsible for rapid processing of meaningful information (such as the presence of danger), while the late response can be related to emotional processing. Indeed, the early response of the amygdala is enhanced when there are predator cues or during fear conditioning. Sounds with different emotional tones can trigger different response patterns in the amygdala. It is well documented that the amygdala plays a crucial role in Pavlovian fear conditioning. During this process, both the conditioned stimulus (CS) and the unconditioned stimulus (US) converge on the neurons in the lateral amygdala (LA), thereby activating the central amygdala (CeA) and triggering the conditioned response. Interestingly, the amygdala can be associated with various psychiatric disorders, such as anxiety disorders, depression, and even tinnitus. The amygdala is composed of the LA, the basal lateral amygdala (BLA), the basal medial amygdala (BMA), the CeA, the medial amygdala (MeA) and the cortical amygdala (CoA). The lateral amygdala complex (LA, BLA and BMA) is mainly composed of glutamatergic pyramidal neurons (PNs, accounting for 70%-85% of the total neurons), while the CeA mainly contains GABAergic neurons (>90% of the neurons). Glutamate and GABA are the two main neurotransmitters in the amygdala. In addition, the neural activity of the amygdala can also be regulated by various neurotransmitters, neuromodulators and hormones from other areas of the brain, such as acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), and glucocorticoids. The LA receives sensory information from both the thalamus (the fast low road) and the cortex (the slow high road). The PNs in the LA can directly stimulate the projection neurons in the CeA, thereby triggering corresponding behavioral responses, such as urgent response or fear conditioning. The LA PNs can also project to the BLA and BMA for further information processing. The PNs in the BLA/BMA can directly project to the CeA or project to the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex for processing. The rapid fear conditioning can be achieved through the fast low road. However, the information processing results through the slow high road may modulate or override the initial fear response through the fast low road. More than 90% of the neurons in the CeA are inhibitory neurons, inhibiting neural activity of the brainstem. For example, in the context of freezing behavior, they can inhibit the neural activity of the pre-Bötzinger complex, thereby suppressing breathing. The CeA also contains excitatory neurons (<10%). They can excite neurons in the hypothalamus or in the caudal pontine reticular nucleus, triggering the fight-or-flight response or leading to an enhanced auditory startle response.

title: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation alleviates post-stroke depressive symptoms by enhancing hippocampal CA1 neuroplasticity via upregulation of ALK5 expression.
abstract: Poststroke depression critically hampers neurological recovery, and although transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation exhibits antidepressant potential, its mechanistic basis remains incompletely defined. Given that activin receptorlike kinase 5 (ALK5) regulates neuroplasticity through the Smad2/3/growth arrest and DNA-damage-inducible 45β (Gadd45b) axis, we postulated that transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation alleviates poststroke depression via this cascade. Using a rat poststroke depression model established by middle cerebral artery occlusion combined with chronic unpredictable mild stress, we knocked down ALK5 in hippocampal CA1 area and administered 14-day transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation. Behavioral assessments, histopathological and ultrastructural analyses, neurotransmitter measurements, and immunoblotting for neuroplasticity markers revealed that transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation reversed post-stroke depression-induced ALK5 downregulation and concurrently ameliorated depressive-like behaviors, restored monoamine levels, and enhanced neuronal survival, dendritic arborization, and synaptic integrity. Crucially, ALK5 knockdown abolished all these beneficial effects and blocked transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulationmediated activation of the Smad2/3/Gadd45b pathway. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation exerts its anti-depressant and proneuroplastic actions in poststroke depression by engaging the hippocampal ALK5 signaling cascade, thereby supporting transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation as a promising therapeutic strategy for poststroke affective and functional recovery.

title: Targeting the central-peripheral-effector muscle axis: Rapamycin promotes functional recovery in injured peripheral nerves.
abstract: Peripheral nerve repair requires not only axonal regeneration and remyelination but also preservation of spinal circuitry and denervated target muscles during the denervation and regenerative period. We investigated whether Rapamycin treatment could improve repair across the central-peripheral-effector muscle axis after sciatic nerve crush injury. Mice were assigned to sham, crush, 3-methyladenine, or rapamycin groups and evaluated using histological, ultrastructural, molecular, transcriptomic, electrophysiological, and behavioral analyses, together with injury-conditioned dorsal root ganglion cultures and RSC96 Schwann cell assays. Rapamycin accelerated axonal extension, enhanced axon maturation and remyelination, improved myelin ultrastructure, and promoted Schwann cell proliferation, migration, and neurite outgrowth. In the spinal cord, rapamycin reduced neuronal apoptosis and glial activation, preserved synaptic markers, and was associated with transcriptional changes involving inflammatory, extracellular matrix remodeling, nociceptive, synaptic, axonal growth, and myelination-related programs. In denervated gastrocnemius muscle, Rapamycin preserved muscle mass and myofiber area, reduced ubiquitin-associated protein degradation, and increased neuromuscular junction reinnervation. These effects were accompanied by changes in autophagy-related markers, including an increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and reduced p62 expression, together with altered mTORC1, AMPK, and AKT signaling. Rapamycin further improved sensory reinnervation, compound muscle action potential amplitude, gait, and motor and sensory recovery. These findings indicate that Rapamycin promotes peripheral nerve repair through multi-level protective effects involving regenerating axons, spinal neural circuitry, and denervated muscle.

title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

title: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles in cell-free therapeutics for neurological diseases.
abstract: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles offer a promising frontier in nanomedicine for managing neurological diseases.
