title: Spatiotemporal AI modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable AI transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 brain regions, 30 cell types, and seven developmental stages. Seal predictions enable characterization of both germline and somatic brain variants, and provide mechanistic interpretation by linking sequence variants to transcriptional regulators in spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify cell types and developmental windows relevant to neuropsychiatric disease risk, revealing shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing a cell-type and developmentally specific regulatory burden. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

title: Regional Similarity to Sex-Typical Young Adult Brain Architecture is a Longitudinal Correlate of Neuroinflammation and Depression in Later Adulthood.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Lifespan trajectories of psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk show robust overlap and marked sex differences. Nonetheless, their neurobiological underpinnings are still poorly understood. One potential culprit is the predominant categorical definition of sex, which overlooks the tapestry of sex-dependent and sex-independent features recently shown to typify each human brain. Shifting from a holistic, dichotomous approach to regionally specific, continuous assessments of sex differences in brain function could help identify individualized therapeutic targets for both psychiatric and neurological conditions. To probe the psychiatric and neurological relevance of functional alignment with sex-typical brain architecture, we analyzed longitudinal neuroimaging and clinical data from a healthy aging cohort (N = 353, aged 36-87 years). We identified complementary patterns of deviance from sex-typical brain architecture along the canonical sensorimotor-to-association axis, which overlapped areas enriched in microglial genes and genes regulating sex steroid metabolism. The two connectivity patterns differentiated longitudinally between psychiatric symptoms and neurodegeneration as a function sex and age: one connectivity pattern related to more severe future depression in younger women, whereas the second related to later neurodegeneration (higher GFAP and pT217 blood concentration) and poorer fluid cognition (inhibition, episodic memory, processing speed, working memory) in older men. The aforementioned effects showed some context-specificity, as they involved connectivity patterns characterized during awake rest and cognitive control, but not associative memory performance. Taken together, our findings attest to the value of integrating regionally specific, continuous assessments of sex differences in brain function with inflammation-relevant biomarkers in order to support precision medicine approaches across the life course.

title: Aging Differentially Remodels the Retina and RPE/Choroid Proteome and Metabolism.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The neural retina and retinal pigment epithelium/choroid (RPE/Cho) are metabolically coupled. Metabolic dysfunction of the RPE/Cho contributes to photoreceptor death in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). This study aimed to determine how aging, a major risk factor for AMD, alters the proteome and metabolic pathways in the retina and RPE/Cho. We performed quantitative proteomics on neural retina and RPE/Cho from young (8-week) and old (73-week) C57BL/6J mice. The differentially expressed proteins between old and young, as well as between the retina and RPE/Cho, were visualized using volcano plots and heatmaps, and functional analyses were assessed by Gene Ontology enrichment tools. Aging altered the expression of 85 retinal proteins and 272 RPE/Cho, with 16 shared between tissues. In the aged retina, proteins associated with NADP(H) metabolism, neurodegeneration, and immunity were mostly upregulated, while proteins in lipid metabolism, transcription, and epigenetic regulation decreased. In the aged RPE/Cho, all 21 significantly altered lysosomal enzymes and transport proteins increased, together with complement components, and photoreceptor outer segment proteins. These changes accompanied increases in proteins associated with lipid metabolism and protection against lipid peroxidation, while several glutathione metabolism enzymes decreased. Seven shared proteins involved in lipid and NADP(H) metabolism, changed in opposite directions between retina and RPE/Cho. Comparison of the retinal and RPE/Cho proteomes identified 3073 differentially abundant proteins, of which 2452 maintained tissue-specific differences across both age groups, while approximately 17% showed age-dependent shifts in tissue enrichment. These shifts involved proteins associated with metabolism, extracellular matrix, visual function, lysosomal pathways, and innate immunity. Within the metabolic proteome, several glycolytic and fatty acid oxidation proteins showed greater relative enrichment in RPE/Cho with age, whereas glucose transporters and mitochondrial complexes shifted toward the retina. Overall, these findings show that aging differentially remodels the retina and RPE/Cho proteome, accompanied by altered metabolic specialization between the two tissues.

title: Blood-brain barrier-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap for anti-cancer immunomodulation of gliomas.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Clinical studies have revealed that glioblastoma (GBM) is refractory to immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) primarily intensified by intratumoral upregulation of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ). Primary GBM tumor bulks are surgically removed in clinic, but invasive tumor cells infiltrated into surrounding normal brain tissue cannot be eradicated by systemic therapy due to the integral blood-brain barrier (BBB), leading to near-inevitable tumor recurrence. To address these translational challenges, we have engineered a TGFβ-inhibiting protein nanocage comprising human heavy-chain ferritin protein and TGFβ receptor II ectodomain that enables BBB penetration and multivalent TGFβ entrapment, respectively. We demonstrate that the nanocage platform, denoted TβR2-HFt, following systemic administration, traverses the BBB, and extensively modulates immunosuppressive TME, both stromal and immune components, thereby potentiating the therapeutic efficacy of a clinically used ICI in multiple mouse glioma models. Notably, a majority of the glioma-bearing animals that received surgical tumor resection, followed by treatment with TβR2-HFt and the ICI, survived the tumor and resisted tumor rechallenge, providing a potential means to control GBM in a durable manner. BBB-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap reverses the immunosuppressive TME to rescue therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade against GBM.

title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [ 11 C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.

title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ∼1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC₅₀=2.22 μM), with comparable potency against Ca v 3.1 (IC 50 =1.63 µM). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception 1-3 . In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing 4-8 . Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear 9-11 . Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

title: Differential utilization of PACAP and glutamate in parabrachial neurons shapes pain and stress responses.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The external parabrachial nucleus (elPBN) contributes to diverse behaviors, including pain and stress. Neurons in this region use glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling, with pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) expressed in a subset of glutamatergic neurons. Deletion of PACAP in elPBN neurons attenuates behavioral responses to stress, but the contribution of PACAP to pain sensitization and of glutamatergic neurotransmission to pain- and stress-related responses are poorly understood. Here, we show that constitutive loss of PACAP markedly attenuated nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity across heat, pressure, cold and tactile modalities without altering baseline nociception, while also reducing inflammation-induced spontaneous pain-related behavior. Selective deletion of PACAP within elPBN neurons phenocopied the suppression of injury-induced hypersensitivity, but left inflammation-induced pain-related behavior unaffected. Ex vivo optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping showed that activation of PACAP-expressing elPBN terminals elicited glutamatergic transmission onto central amygdala (CeA) PKCδ-expressing neurons. Selective deletion of VGluT2 in elPBN neurons reduced nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity but, unlike PACAP deletion, also reduced inflammation-induced pain-related behavior, while leaving stress-induced hypophagia intact. Together, these findings reveal differential requirements for PACAP and glutamatergic neurotransmission within the elPBN to allow pain- and stress-related behaviors. The parabrachial nucleus contributes to pain and stress responses through neurons that express multiple neurotransmitters. Here, we show that disrupting PACAP or glutamatergic signaling in the elPBN produces distinct effects across nerve injury-induced sensitization, inflammation-induced pain-related behavior, and restraint stress-induced hypophagia. These findings reveal functional specialization of signaling mechanisms within the elPBN, highlighting neurotransmitter diversity as an important feature of its broad behavioral functions.

title: Multiscale Network Disruption of Auditory-Language Circuits Underlying Auditory Hallucinations in Schizophrenia.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH) are among the most disabling symptoms of schizophrenia, yet the network-level mechanisms linking auditory dysfunction to hallucination severity remain poorly characterized, limiting targeted therapeutic development. Using resting-state fMRI and high-resolution surface-based parcellation (HCP-MMP), we examined auditory-language functional connectivity and mesoscale network organization in 56 patients with schizophrenia and 22 healthy controls (primary dataset, N=78). Pairwise auditory-language connectivity associations with hallucination severity (PANSS P3) were examined alongside auditory network community structure, assortativity, hub organization, and routing efficiency. To further characterize these parcel-level findings at the vertex level, we applied a region-growing approach to identify auditory-frontal connectivity patterns maximally associated with severity. In silico perturbation analyses tested the causal role of belt cortex connectivity. Key findings were independently replicated in 93 patients from the Human Connectome Project for Early Psychosis (HCP-EP), for a combined total of 171 participants. Auditory-language connectivity disruptions were concentrated in belt cortex and specifically implicated ventral what-stream connections, with a vertex-wise analysis converging on the same anatomy. Auditory network segregation scaled with hallucination severity, with belt cortex emerging as the primary integrative hub governing auditory-to-language routing efficiency. Perturbation analyses showed that strengthening earlier-hierarchy auditory regions reduced network segregation more than strengthening later-hierarchy regions. Reduced belt cortex coupling and elevated network segregation replicated independently in the HCP-EP sample. Auditory network disorganization scales with hallucination severity and replicates across independent samples, with belt cortex as the critical locus of connectivity disruption and network integration failure, identifying it as a candidate neuromodulatory target.

title: EthoTrace: from behaviour to neural dynamics in a unified analysis system.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Understanding how neural populations support natural behaviour requires knowing what a population does while an animal performs a specific, self-initiated action. For responses evoked by an experimenter-delivered stimulus, the signal can be aligned by the trigger itself, and no behavioural scoring is needed to define the event. Complex behaviours such as parental care and social interaction provide no such trigger. They are defined from the video record, usually offline and post hoc, and are conventionally scored in one program and exported to another for analysis. In this study we developed EthoTrace, a single self-contained HTML file that runs in a desktop browser without installation, server or network access and carries a session from behaviour and calcium signal through to the statistical comparison. Behaviour is annotated on a timeline shared with the ΔF/F trace, the signal is corrected and scaled under a stated baseline convention, single bouts stay inspectable in their behavioural context, and repeated bouts are aligned without filling absent data. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a parenting behaviour experiment, in which behaviour was scored and the photometry signal analysed in a single session folder. We expect EthoTrace to facilitate integrative analysis in neuroscience, where behavioural observation and fiber photometry signals are interpreted together.

title: An astrocytic AMPAR-dependent parity signal preserves synaptic strength.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Astrocytic processes closely associate with excitatory synapses and express AMPARs, positioning them to sense the same glutamate signals as neurons. Whether a mismatch between neuronal and astrocytic glutamate sensing affects synaptic physiology is unknown. Using AstroHTP, an extension of Drug Acutely Restricted by Tethering (DART) for cell-type-specific pharmacology, we found that acute astrocytic AMPAR inhibition spared neuronal AMPARs and basal transmission yet converted ongoing glutamatergic activity into a remarkably potent form of long-term depression (LTD) in mouse striatal projection neurons (SPNs). Unlike canonical presynaptic LTD, this form of LTD manifests postsynaptically, requires non-ionotropic NMDA receptor signaling, and arises when glutamate transmission occurs without a matching astrocytic signal. Astrocytic glutamate sensing through AMPARs, therefore, acts as a parity signal that verifies transmission and stabilizes active synapses.

title: The microbial soy metabolite S-equol mitigates cadmium neurotoxicity in mice.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Environmental exposures are major but understudied determinants of chronic disease. Cadmium is a pervasive toxic metal encountered through diet and tobacco smoke that has been associated with cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease mortality, yet strategies to mitigate its neurotoxicity remain limited. S-equol is a gut microbial metabolite of soy daidzein that crosses the blood brain barrier and preferentially activates estrogen receptor beta. Here, we show that cadmium disrupts an axis linking the equol producing gut bacterium Adlercreutzia equolifaciens to circulating S-equol and hippocampal estrogen receptor expression in mice, that S-equol attenuates cadmium-induced cytotoxicity and restores neuronal, glutamatergic and synaptic transcriptional programs in mouse neural progenitor cells, and that circulating S-equol in older humans is lower in apolipoprotein E4 carriers and covaries with body mass index, identifying S-equol as a microbiome-derived, host-modulated candidate countermeasure against cadmium neurotoxicity.

title: The anterior insular cortex mediates higher-order threat learning and memory.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Learning about potential threats is indispensable for survival, and its deficits underlie numerous neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain imaging suggests the anterior insular cortex (AIC) as a key neural correlate of threat learning, yet its mechanistic role remains unclear. Leveraging multimodal systems neuroscience approaches, we demonstrate that AIC excitatory neurons, specifically layer 5 pyramidal neurons projecting to the basolateral amygdala, are essential for higher-order threat learning/memory. They are specifically required when a predictor is temporally separated from an aversive event or when the predictive information is embedded within a diffuse context. In contrast, the AIC is dispensable for elementary, temporally contiguous threat learning. Surprisingly, while the AIC promotes memory formation, it also constrains the level of fear expression during retrieval in a context-dependent manner. This bidirectional control is mediated by the recruitment of distinct AIC neuronal ensembles. Together, we identify a novel circuit mechanism for bidirectional regulation of higher-order threat learning/memory.

title: Pathological tau leads to network hyperexcitability through neuronal-subtype-specific functional impairment.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Pathological tau disrupts neuronal activity and brain function in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies. However, the underlying mechanisms for neuronal network dysfunction remain largely unknown. Using human inducible pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) - derived neurons, we show that the familial MAPT P301L mutation leads to neuronal network hyperexcitability. Imbalanced excitation and inhibition were attributable to neuronal subtype-specific tau pathology that was associated with different alterations of tau interactomes in excitatory versus inhibitory neurons. Suppressing enhanced excitatory synaptic transmission or blocking Ca 2+ influx resulting from enhanced P301L tau/AHNAK interaction in inhibitory neurons rescued the neuronal network hyperexcitability. This study expands our understanding on how disease-causing tau mutations alter the excitatory/inhibitory balance, leading to network dysfunction in human neurons. The FTD-causing P301L tau mutation leads to neuronal network hyperexcitability.P301L tau causes hyperactivity of excitatory neurons while hypoactivity of inhibitory neurons.Tau and P301L tau interactomes differ in excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons.Enhanced excitatory synaptic transmission and P301L tau/AHNAK interaction in inhibitory neurons contribute to neuronal network hyperexcitability.

title: Dual ecological-cultural pathways of sociocultural environment and resting state functional connectivity among Hispanic adolescents in the ABCD Study.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Hispanic Americans face persistent health disparities rooted in complex sociocultural and bioecodevelopmental dynamics. Identifying early neurodevelopmental trajectories that confer risk or resilience during adolescence is critical for developing targeted health equity interventions. Grounded in the NIMHD Research Framework and bioecodevelopmental theory, data from 12- to 14-year-old Hispanic adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study were analyzed (n=236). Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) was used to evaluate multivariate associations between sociocultural measures-spanning individual, family, and community levels-and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) networks. Post hoc linear mixed-effects models examined how derived sociocultural-rsFC patterns predicted measures of physical and mental health, linking bioecodevelopmental patterns to adolescent well-being. PLSC revealed dual community- and family-level neural pathways of biological embedding, diverging from traditional nested bioecodevelopmental assumptions. The community pathway linked child opportunity and neighborhood disadvantage to connectivity across Cingulo-Opercular, Default, Dorsal Attention, Visual Networks. This community-rsFC profile was associated with lower respiratory functioning, reflecting an allostatic load marker of environmental stress. The family pathway linked caregiver ethnic identity and heritage acculturation to Default, Ventral Attention, Sensorimotor-Mouth, and Visual Networks connectivity, suggesting that the family system shapes neural systems underlying social attunement and identity formation. Structural community factors and familial culture impose distinct neurobiological demands on the adolescent connectome among Hispanic youth. Findings highlight respiratory health as a biological marker of environmental adversity and underscore the necessity of structural and culturally sustaining interventions to promote health equity among Hispanic youth.

title: Epigenome Alterations and 3D Chromatin Architecture Remodeling in Inflammatory Macrophage Activation under Diabetic Conditions.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Aberrant monocyte/macrophage activation in diabetes drives chronic inflammation and diabetic complications. Although epigenetic mechanisms are implicated in these processes, the contribution of three-dimensional (3D) chromatin reorganization remains unclear. Here, we use integrated multi-omics approaches to profile gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin architecture in human CD14⁺ monocyte-derived macrophages exposed to high glucose and TNF-α (HT), mimicking the diabetic milieu. HT induces inflammatory transcription programs that recapitulate those observed in diabetes and dynamically remodel chromatin accessibility, enhancer-promoter interactions, and topologically associated domains. Inflammatory genes exhibit increased chromatin accessibility, whereas cell cycle and metabolic genes display reduced accessibility and weakened enhancer-promoter interactions. These architectural changes promote the convergence of lineage-determining and signal-dependent transcription factors at enhancer-promoter loops, generating distinct regulatory hubs that orchestrate pro-inflammatory responses. Similar enhancer-promoter interactions are observed in peripheral blood derived monocytes from individuals with diabetes. Furthermore, perturbing chromatin interactions via CRISPR interference targeting HT-induced enhancers suppresses nearby CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Collectively, this first comprehensive enhancer connectome map of macrophages under diabetic conditions advances the field by revealing extensive disease-associated rewiring of the 3D epigenome, highlighting chromatin architecture and epigenetic mechanisms as potential therapeutic target for diabetes-associated inflammation. In diabetes, high glucose (Glc) and inflammatory cytokines remodel macrophage 3D chromatin architecture and enhancer connectomes, altering enhancer-promoter interactions, facilitating the convergence of lineage-specific and signal-dependent transcription factors (such as NF-κB) that regulate inflammatory factors associated with macrophage activation. This can promote chronic inflammation and accelerate diabetic complications. Targeted enhancer editing strategies could enable new epigenetic therapies to mitigate chronic inflammatory diabetes complications.

title: Pharmacokinetic properties of Ogerin and its regulation of post-ischemia signaling in mice.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Ogerin, a positive regulator of GPR68, reduces infarct volume and attenuates blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage post transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). These data support the potential use of Ogerin for ischemic protection. For therapeutic interventions, tissue distribution, kinetics, and brain penetration are important characteristics for a compound. For these reasons, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of Ogerin in mice. At 3 hours following intraperitoneal (IP) injection, liver exhibited highest level of Ogerin among all major organs assessed. We further analyzed time-dependent changes in Ogerin concentration in serum following intravenous delivery. Brain Ogerin level was ∼140 ng/g at 2 hour and ∼0.06ng/g at 24 hours. The brain-to-serum ratio of Ogerin was ∼0.6 at 5 hr. To determine the effect of Ogerin on signaling, we collected samples 24 hours after tMCAO with or without Ogerin delivered and performed Western blotting. Consistent with the diminished level of Ogerin in brain at 24 hour, tMCAO increased similar changes in phosphorylation of PKA substrates and PKC substrates in vehicle- and Ogerin-treated groups. The pharmacokinetic data suggests that Ogerin is effective mainly during acute hours after injection. This finding generates important insights on the design of effective protocol for Ogerin delivery to potentiate GPR68 function in vivo.

title: Extended amygdala function is governed by threat probability, not uncertainty.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Anxiety is a universal experience that arises as we anticipate negative events that may or may not happen. When extreme, anxiety is a major cause of distress, suffering, and disability-adjusted life years, with nearly one in four individuals experiencing clinically relevant anxiety in their lifetime 1-3 . Elucidating the biological basis of anxiety has the potential to help people understand, cope with, and ultimately receive improved treatments for their anxiety. The canonical neuroscientific model of anxiety posits that distinct regions of the extended amygdala (EA) elicit distress that is conditional on threat uncertainty 4 . Here, we refute this model using a precise computational framework to disambiguate specific dimensional facets of threat uncertainty in a racially diverse sample of 104 individuals. We show that self-report, psychophysiological, and neural correlates of threat anticipation are much more strongly associated with threat probability than uncertainty per se . Importantly, EA regions, including the central nucleus of the amygdala (Ce) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST), were most reliably associated with threat probability-contrary to the canonical model. Re-examination of the pioneering experiments that motivated the canonical model reveal a previously unappreciated confound between probability and uncertainty, suggesting the novel hypothesis that EA regions differ in their sensitivity to low-probability threats. Our fMRI data support this, showing that BST is more sensitive to low-probability threats than Ce. Moreover, lesion experiments in rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ) demonstrate that BST causally contributes to defensive behavior in low-probability threat contexts. Together, these data reconcile previous empirical inconsistencies, provide a fresh theoretical perspective on the neurobiology of anxiety, and underscore the theoretical importance of a formal lingua franca for coordinated cross-species emotion research.

title: Overexpressing FLP Recombinase Can Cause Synaptic Trafficking Defects in C. elegans.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Site-specific recombinases, such as Cre recombinase (Cre) and FLP recombinase (FLPase), are popular tools that enable precise spatiotemporal control over fluorescent reporter genes. However, studies show that increased Cre expression can lead to cytotoxic phenotypes including DNA damage, cell cycle arrest, cell death, and aneuploidy. In contrast, there is little-to-no known cytotoxicity associated with FLPase. FLPase is considered to be the safer, if less efficient, recombinase. To compensate for decreased efficiency, researchers will often increase expression of the FLPase to ensure a complete gene edit. Despite previous evidence that FLPase is nontoxic at high doses, we report that high expression of FLPase from multi-copy extrachromosomal arrays can disrupt synaptic protein trafficking in C. elegans . We discovered several off-target effects of high FLPase expression including mislocalization of the pre-synaptic marker FLPon::mScarlet::SYD-2 and decreased synaptic abundance, transport, and expression of the ionotropic glutamate receptor subunit GLR-1. Neither overexpression of an inactive FLPase, low activity FLPase, nor mCherry under the same promoter elicited these effects. However, single- copy expression of the FLPase construct reliably tags FLPon::mScarlet::SYD-2 and does not lead to these off-target effects. This work supports growing awareness that tyrosine recombinases can become cytotoxic at high doses.

title: Axonal dysfunction precedes axonal degeneration in a mouse model of progressive parkinsonism.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Axons of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons "die back" in Parkinson's disease (PD), exhibiting early degeneration relative to cell bodies, a key feature also observed in PD models. A critical step towards understanding the process of axonal neurodegeneration is to determine the physiological properties of dopaminergic axons that are altered during the early stages of cellular dysfunction. Here, we compared the electrophysiology and calcium dynamics of dopaminergic axons in the MitoPark model of PD with age-matched controls. Our experiments show a pronounced reduction in action potential (AP)-evoked calcium signals in MitoPark axons that emerges well before the onset of dopaminergic fiber loss and motor deficits. In addition, calcium imaging and direct axon recording revealed deficits in AP propagation accompanied by alterations in the axonal AP waveform. Therefore, our experimental findings identify the progression of axon-specific physiological deficits that occur long before neurodegeneration, more precisely defining the period that precedes axonal loss.

title: Netrin signaling shapes sexually dimorphic neurite branching of a sex-shared interneuron in C. elegans.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Sexually dimorphic behaviors arise from underlying differences in neural circuit architecture between the sexes, yet the molecular mechanisms that establish these structural differences remain poorly understood. In Caenorhabditis elegans , the sex-shared interneuron AVG exhibits sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity, offering a model for investigating the development of sexually dimorphic neuronal morphology. Here, we identified that AVG displays male-specific neurite branching and demonstrated that the conserved axon guidance cue UNC-6/Netrin and its receptor UNC-40/DCC are essential for this structural remodeling. Cell-specific manipulation of sexual identity revealed that male identity confers branching competence to AVG. Loss of UNC-6 or UNC-40 abolished branch formation, whereas loss of the alternate Netrin receptor UNC-5/Unc5 had no detectable effect. Cell-specific rescue experiments showed that UNC-40 functions in AVG through its UNC-6 binding domains. Furthermore, genetic ablation of the male-specific presynaptic neuron PCA, which expresses unc-6 , diminished AVG branch length, establishing PCA as a candidate local source of UNC-6. Together, our findings support a model in which presynaptic UNC-6/Netrin cues from male-specific neurons promote dimorphic neurite branching in sex-shared neurons, illustrating how evolutionarily conserved signaling molecules are redeployed during sexual maturation to sculpt sex-specific neural circuits.

title: Biophysical modeling of excitation/inhibition imbalance in Alzheimer's disease.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves early sensory and perceptual changes that can precede memory decline. We developed a two-layer rate-based neural model of early and higher visual areas with feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections to examine how excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance shapes visual motion perception in AD. Using Motion-Induced Position Shift and Altered Motion Repulsion stimuli, we factorially manipulated excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) subfield power and connectivity to examine their effects on illusion representation across visual layers. Increased E, decreased I, and increased E/I reduced illusion representation, consistent with reduced illusion susceptibility in AD, whereas the converse increased illusion representation, reflecting neurotypical processing. Higher-level layer 2 representations were more resistant to E/I perturbations than lower-level layer 1. Illusion representation was less affected by E/I increases in intra-areal (recurrent) connectivity than in inter-areal (feedforward/feedback) connectivity. This mechanistic framework links E/I balance and connectivity to altered visual motion illusion representations in AD and suggests that E/I and connectivity measures may provide probes of early AD neurobiology. The framework may also generalize beyond vision.

title: Triple-Omics Analysis Unveiled the Neuroprotective Mechanisms of Akkermansia muciniphila in an Environmental Exposure-Linked Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is an emerging environmental risk factor for cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease, and few interventions limit its effects on the brain. Akkermansia muciniphila , a human gut commensal, is neuroprotective through mechanisms that remain unclear. Building on our finding that A. muciniphila prevented Cd-induced memory deficits without reducing brain Cd burden (Wang et al., 2026a), we tested whether it reprograms Cd-disrupted hippocampal RNA regulation. Male C57BL/6J mice received A. muciniphila (1×10⁹ CFU, oral gavage, 5 days/week) before and throughout 9 weeks of 3 mg/L CdCl₂ exposure; hippocampi were analyzed by RNA-seq, m⁶A epitranscriptomic profiling, and rMATS-based alternative-splicing analysis. Cd disrupted hippocampal neuropeptide signaling, neuronal excitability, and synaptic plasticity. Co-exposure with A. muciniphila reversed signatures enriched for Nrf2-centered cytoprotective signaling and opposed m⁶A and splicing changes across more than a thousand genes, largely without changes in total mRNA abundance. Restored events converged on machinery governing local translation, calcium-dependent plasticity, and synaptic transmission. Projected onto predicted protein structures, most introduced a premature termination codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay or edited short loop and linker segments rather than rebuilding folded domains, regulation largely invisible to gene-level expression analysis. Among these, paired events amplifying semaphorin-plexin signaling, an axis linked to oligodendrocyte injury and memory consolidation, were reversed. These findings identify restoration of hippocampal transcript fate and splice-isoform selection as a mechanism potentially underlying A. muciniphila -mediated protection against Cd neurotoxicity, and establish post-transcriptional RNA regulation as a gut-brain target for mitigating environmentally driven neurotoxicity. Cadmium is a widespread environmental contaminant associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease, and few interventions are available to limit its effects on the brain. This study shows that supplementation with the gut commensal Akkermansia muciniphila reverses Cd-induced changes in hippocampal m⁶A methylation and splice-isoform selection, largely without altering total transcript abundance. These results identify post-transcriptional RNA regulation as a gut-brain target for mitigating environmentally driven neurotoxicity, and show that conventional gene-expression analysis alone would miss most of the protective response.

title: A Bayesian functional model with multilevel partition priors for group studies in neuroscience.
abstract: The statistical analysis of group studies in neuroscience is particularly challenging due to the complex spatio-temporal nature of the data, its multiple levels and the inter-individual variability in brain responses. Traditional ANOVA-based studies and linear mixed effects models typically provide only a limited exploration of the dynamics of group brain activity and of the variability in individual responses, potentially leading to overly simplistic conclusions and/or missing more intricate patterns. In this study we propose a novel Bayesian model-based clustering approach for functional data that simultaneously assesses group effects and individual deviations across the main temporal features in the data. To this end, we develop a multilevel partition prior to model the functional scores arising from a functional Principal Components decomposition of neuroscientific recordings. The proposed approach enables a thorough exploration of group differences and individual deviations without compromising on the spatio-temporal nature of the data. Through a simulation study we demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves correct classification in different clustering scenarios under low and high noise levels in the data. Finally, we consider an Electroencephalogram case study involving an object recognition task, where the proposed approach provides new insights into the underlying brain mechanisms generating the data and their variability.
